questions.q: If an attacker took one server today, how many others could it reach?
questions.why: Lateral movement is how one compromised machine becomes a breach.
questions.need: The reach of one compromised server is known, and limited to what its application needs
questions.how: Map what one critical server can reach today and agree what it should reach
questions.listen: If nobody knows, the answer is usually most of them.
questions.probe: In the last penetration test, how far did the testers get from one machine?

questions.q: Which audit or regulation asks you to separate environments, and how do you prove it today?
questions.why: Evidence for auditors turns a security wish into a budget line.
questions.need: The separation required by audit is known, with the evidence it needs
questions.how: List the requirements and the evidence each auditor expects
questions.listen: Payment, health or critical-infrastructure rules make separation a requirement with a deadline.
questions.probe: When is the next audit, and what did the last one find?

questions.q: Can you see which machines talk to which inside the data centre?
questions.why: Policies cannot be written for traffic nobody can see.
questions.need: East-west traffic is visible for every environment in scope
questions.how: Turn on traffic visibility, without enforcing anything, for each environment
questions.listen: Without seeing the flows, rules are guesses: start by watching.
questions.probe: How long would it take to list every connection to the most sensitive database?

questions.q: Are machines labelled by application, environment and role, or only known by their address?
questions.why: Policies written on addresses break when machines move; policies on labels follow them.
questions.need: Machines carry labels that policies can use, kept up to date by their owners
questions.how: Agree a labelling scheme and label the applications in scope
questions.listen: Rules written on addresses break when machines move; labels survive.
questions.probe: Who owns the naming and labelling standard?

questions.q: Are test and production kept apart, or only on different address ranges?
questions.why: Address ranges are not a control; an isolation policy is.
questions.need: Environments are isolated by policy, and the isolation is tested
questions.how: Write isolation policies between environments and test a blocked connection
questions.listen: Separated only by address ranges means one mistake joins them.
questions.probe: Can a test machine reach a production database today?

questions.q: Could you isolate a machine suspected of compromise in a minute, and still investigate it?
questions.why: Containment time decides how far an attacker gets.
questions.need: A suspect machine can be quarantined in one step, with forensic access kept
questions.how: Prepare quarantine policies and rehearse one on a test machine
questions.listen: A quarantine that keeps the machine for investigation beats switching it off.
questions.probe: What did the incident team do the last time a machine was suspected?

questions.q: Do security policies follow a machine when it moves or fails over to another site?
questions.why: A recovery site without the same policies is an open door during the worst day.
questions.need: Policies follow workloads across hosts, sites and failover
questions.how: Test a policy before and after a migration and a failover
questions.listen: Policies left behind after a failover open a gap at the worst moment.
questions.probe: What happens to firewall rules when a machine fails over today?

questions.q: Who decides on a blocked connection that an application needs, and how quickly?
questions.why: Enforcement without an owner turns into exceptions nobody reviews.
questions.need: A named owner reviews blocked connections and exceptions, with a response time
questions.how: Name the owner and agree how requests for new flows are handled
questions.listen: Slow exceptions push teams to ask for broad rules; a fast path keeps rules narrow.
questions.probe: How long does a firewall change take today, from request to done?

questions.q: Which firewalls and network tools control traffic between machines inside the data centre today?
questions.why: Existing tools may be kept, connected or replaced.
questions.need: Controls on traffic inside the data centre are listed with owners
questions.how: List the firewalls and policies that control traffic between machines
questions.listen: Traffic between machines on the same network often passes no control at all.
questions.probe: How many rules does the core firewall hold, and how many are never used?

questions.q: Which applications should be protected first, and who knows how they talk?
questions.why: Starting with a few critical applications makes progress visible.
questions.need: The first applications to protect are chosen with their owners
questions.how: Pick three applications and map their flows with their owners
questions.listen: Protecting a few critical applications well beats a plan for everything that never starts.
questions.probe: Which application would hurt most if an attacker reached it?

questions.q: Can a policy first run in watch mode, logging what it would block, before it enforces?
questions.why: Watching first lets teams build rules without outages.
questions.need: Policies are tried in watch mode before they enforce
questions.how: Agree a watch period per application before enforcing
questions.listen: Fear of outages is the main brake; a watch period removes it.
questions.probe: What happened the last time a firewall change broke an application?

questions.q: What would a breach that spread from machine to machine cost, and has an insurer asked how you contain one?
questions.why: Insurers and boards now ask how far one incident could spread, and the answer prices the risk.
questions.need: How far one incident could spread, and what it would cost, can be answered with evidence
questions.how: Put a figure on one spreading incident with finance, and list what the insurer asked
questions.listen: An insurer's questionnaire or a premium that rose makes this concrete; "we have a firewall" means nobody has priced it.
questions.probe: What did the insurer ask at the last renewal, and what did you answer?

questions.q: Which kinds of workload must the separation cover: virtual machines, containers, bare metal, desktops?
questions.why: A policy that covers only one kind of workload leaves the others as a way round it.
questions.need: Every kind of workload that holds or handles sensitive data is covered by the same policies
questions.how: List the kinds of workload around the first applications to protect, and how each connects today
questions.listen: Several kinds named, with one owner for the policy; "only the VMs" leaves containers and bare metal open.
questions.probe: Which of those could be used to get around a policy on the virtual machines?

questions.q: Who is alerted when a machine tries a connection its policy forbids, and what do they do next?
questions.why: A blocked attempt is often the first sign of someone moving inside who should not be there.
questions.need: Forbidden connection attempts go to someone who investigates them
questions.how: Send the blocked connections to the security monitoring, and name who looks at them
questions.listen: Alerts sent to the security team with a named owner; "it is in the logs" means nobody looks.
questions.probe: When did a blocked connection last lead to an investigation?
